notes.meaning: As David crossed the summit of the Mount of Olives, Ziba met him with donkeys carrying bread, raisins, summer fruit, and wine. Ziba was the steward of Saul's grandson Mephibosheth, but he came alone to offer these supplies. His gift seemed generous, but he was secretly laying a trap for his own future gain.

When David asked why he brought these things, Ziba explained that the donkeys were for the royal family to ride and the food was for the young men. The wine was meant to revive anyone who grew faint in the dry wilderness. In ancient court custom, describing gifts this way was a polite sign of deep respect for the king.

David asked where Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was, and Ziba claimed his master had stayed behind in Jerusalem. Ziba told the king that Mephibosheth hoped the people would now restore Saul's kingdom to him. This was a slanderous lie, taking cruel advantage of a lame man who could not travel on his own.

Believing Ziba's story without checking the facts, David impulsively gave all of Mephibosheth's land to Ziba. Ziba bowed low, pretending humble gratitude for the king's favor. In his grief and distress, David acted hastily and made an unfair decision that rewarded a liar.

As David neared the village of Bahurim, a relative of King Saul named Shimei came out shouting curses. Bahurim was in the territory of Benjamin, Saul's home tribe, where bitter feelings toward David still lingered. Shimei seized this moment of David's weakness to vent his long-held hatred.

Shimei threw stones at David and his royal officials as they walked along the path. David was surrounded by his bodyguard and mighty warriors, which made Shimei's attack reckless and bold. The stones were a sign of utter contempt, showing that Shimei thought David deserved to be executed.

Shimei shouted insults, calling David a wicked man and a man of bloodshed who deserved to be driven out. He claimed David had stolen the throne and had blood on his hands. While David had sinned regarding Uriah, Shimei wrongly blamed him for violently wiping out Saul's family.

Shimei told David that the Lord was now punishing him for all the deaths in Saul's household by giving the kingdom to Absalom. He viewed Absalom's rebellion as God's revenge against David. In truth, David had shown great mercy to Saul's family and had not taken the throne by murder.

Abishai, David's fierce nephew and commander, asked why this worthless man should be allowed to curse the king. He called Shimei a 'dead dog,' an expression meaning someone vile and powerless. Abishai asked for permission to cross over the ravine and cut off Shimei's head right away.

David refused Abishai's request and told him not to interfere. He realized that God might be using Shimei's cruel insults as part of his chastening for past sins. Rather than taking personal revenge, David submitted his heart to the Lord's discipline.

David pointed out to his soldiers that his own son Absalom was trying to kill him. If his own flesh and blood sought his life, it was no surprise that a man from Saul's rival tribe would do the same. David ordered his men to let Shimei curse, recognizing God's permissive hand in his trouble.

David hoped that the Lord would see his deep sorrow and show him mercy. He believed that if he patiently endured these wrongful curses without retaliating, God might repay him with blessing instead. Trusting God's justice allowed David to bear insults with quiet hope.

David and his men continued marching along the valley road while Shimei followed on the ridge opposite them. Shimei kept up a steady stream of curses, hurling stones and throwing clouds of dirt into the air. David chose to walk on in silence rather than striking back.

Exhausted by their hurried journey and heavy grief, the king and his followers finally stopped to rest and regain their strength. God provided a safe place for them to recover from their weariness. Even in their lowest hour, the Lord sustained them with needed rest.

Meanwhile, Absalom and a large following of Israelites marched into Jerusalem, accompanied by the trusted counselor Ahithophel. Absalom quickly took control of the capital city just as David had expected. Having the wise Ahithophel on his side gave Absalom great confidence that his rebellion would succeed.

David's loyal friend Hushai came to Absalom and greeted him by shouting, 'Long live the king!' Absalom assumed the greeting was meant for him as the new ruler. In reality, Hushai's words were carefully chosen to support the true king, David, while infiltrating Absalom's inner circle.

Absalom questioned Hushai, asking why he was not loyal to his close friend David. He wondered why Hushai had stayed behind instead of fleeing into the wilderness with the former king. Absalom was testing Hushai's honesty before deciding whether to trust him.

Hushai replied that he would serve the one chosen by the Lord and by all the people of Israel. His answer sounded like full loyalty to Absalom, but it carried a hidden double meaning. Hushai knew in his heart that God had truly chosen David, not Absalom, to be king.

Hushai added that it made sense for him to serve the son just as he had served the father. He presented himself as a faithful servant to the royal house rather than to one particular man. Absalom was flattered by these clever words and welcomed Hushai into his council.

Once established in the palace, Absalom called his first council and asked Ahithophel what their next move should be. He wanted practical advice on how to secure his grip on the kingdom. Instead of seeking guidance from God through the priests, Absalom put all his trust in human wisdom.

Ahithophel advised Absalom to sleep with the concubines David had left behind to tend the palace. In the ancient world, taking a former king's secondary wives was a public claim to his throne. Ahithophel knew this shocking act would make peace between father and son impossible, forcing Absalom's supporters to fight to the end.

Absalom followed this wicked advice by pitching a tent on the palace roof and sleeping with his father's concubines in plain view of all Israel. This fulfilled God's warning through the prophet Nathan that David's secret sin would be punished openly before the whole nation. The very roof where David had first lusted after Bathsheba became the public stage for his family's humiliation.

In those days, people treated Ahithophel's advice with the same respect as a direct message from God. Both David and Absalom had valued his counsel because his plans were usually brilliant and successful. Yet in this crisis, his godless wisdom led Absalom into shameful sin and set the stage for their ruin.
